Animal studies suggest that modification of the protein source from animal to soya protein might slow renal disease progression, especially at high intakes.5 Generally, low-protein diets providing between 0.6 to 0.8 g/kg daily have been recommended,1,6-8 although a very low-protein diet providing 0.3 g of vegetable origin protein, supplemented with a mixture of essential amino acids, has been recommended for highly motivated patients with advanced renal failure.1 Once the patient starts dialysis, however, protein losses through the dialysis membrane or peritoneum may require an increase of protein intake to between 1.2 and 1.3 g/kg daily.6,8 Because ener- gy intake needs to remain constant, food selection has to change qualitatively.6 Sodium, potassium and phosphate intake also need to be controlled.6,8 During dialysis, restricting dietary phos- phate while maintaining sufficient protein intake may be diffi- cult, and modification of the protein source may be necessary.9 After kidney transplantation, if renal function stabilises, protein restriction is again advisable;6 between 1.3 and 1.5 g/kg daily is recommended initially, then 1 g/kg daily for maintenance.8 However, adverse effects of immunosuppressant drugs may complicate the dietary targets, with the patient at risk of diabetes, dyslipidaemia, and possible hypertension.6 The importance of salt restriction and reduction of the sodium dialysate content in controlling hypertension in renal patients has been emphasised.10 It has been suggested that the benefit of other interventions such as the use of ACE inhibitors,11 as well as the difficulties in ob- taining patient compliance with such a restrictive diet,12 may have limited the benefits to be obtained from protein restriction, but there is also evidence that response and outcome vary de- pending on the cause of renal failure.3,13 1.
